backups.name: Twin Sisters Olivine Scramble
backups.fa: Dallas Kloke and Dave Dixon, September 1972 (first ascent of the peak)
hazards: Unbridged/washed-out Middle Fork Nooksack River crossing near the Elbow Lake trailhead (log/rope crossing destroyed in Dec 2025 floods)
Loose, choss-filled rock on Skookum's south-facing slopes — avoid for descent
Exposed, knife-edge ridge scrambling with substantial fall potential, especially on the north ridge variation
backups.overview: Skookum Peak is one of the summits of the Twin Sisters Range west of Mount Baker, a chain famous for its reddish-orange olivine (dunite) rock — a rare exposed fragment of the earth's mantle and the largest such body in the Western Hemisphere. The peak lies on the ridge system extending south from South Twin, the range highpoint, and is a highlight of the popular east-side Green Creek Circuit linkup with South Twin, Jaws' Tooth, Little Sister, and Cinderella. It is also known unofficially as 'Kloke Peak': in 2022 Washington's Committee on Geographic Names took up a proposal to formally rename it after Anacortes climber Dallas Kloke, who with Dave Dixon made the first recorded ascent in September 1972 and put up a dozen new routes across the Twin Sisters through the 1980s before his death in a 2010 North Cascades climbing accident. Both names are still used interchangeably by climbers (commonly written 'Skookum (Kloke)').
backups.beta: The north ridge climbs sustained but famously 'bomber' red dunite/olivine rock rated 5.4, with immense exposure on knife-edge sections; climbers work along small ledges, shuffling hands on positive edges. It is reached by rappelling off the adjacent Jaws' Tooth rather than climbed as a stand-alone route, and continues onward toward Little Sister as one leg of the range's classic 'Green Creek Circuit' traverse.
backups.turnaround: Because the line is committing once past Jaws' Tooth, turn back (or reconsider starting) before that point if conditions, party pace, or weather put finishing the full ridge traverse and the river crossing back at the trailhead in question — there is no fast retreat from Skookum itself.
backups.permit: No climbing permit; a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Elbow Lake Trail's north trailhead.
obj_haz: long approach with an unbridged river ford

waypoints.name: Elbow Lake Trail - North Trailhead (FR 38)
waypoints.note: Low-elevation trailhead off FR 38 via Mosquito Lake Rd; Northwest Forest Pass required, and FR 38 is gated Dec 1-Jun 15 at Wallace Creek. This is a separate trailhead from 'Pioneer Camp,' which sits at the trail's south end off Baker Lake Highway/FSR 12.
waypoints.directions: From the Mount Baker Ranger District office in Sedro-Woolley, drive north on WA-9 to Acme and turn right (east) onto Mosquito Lake Road for about 9 miles, crossing the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then continue onto Forest Road 38 for roughly 11 miles to the north trailhead for the Elbow Lake Trail at about 2,000 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and FR 38 is gated at Wallace Creek from December 1 through June 15. Do not confuse this with the Pioneer Camp trailhead, which sits at the trail's south end off the Baker Lake Highway (FSR 12). As of mid-2026 FR 38 was damaged in the December 2025 floods with no published repair date, so confirm current road conditions with the Mount Baker Ranger District before you drive in.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River crossing
waypoints.note: No bridge on this side — the unofficial log crossing with rope handrails was destroyed in the December 2025 floods and has not been replaced, so this is a ford that can be unfordable at high flow.

waypoints.name: Green Creek climbers' path junction (Hildebrand Creek switchback)
waypoints.note: Unmaintained, sparsely blue-blazed climbers' trail for Green Creek Cirque splits off the maintained Elbow Lake Trail #697 at a switchback near Hildebrand Creek — easy to walk past, watch for paint blazes and flagging.

waypoints.name: Green Creek at the cirque mouth
waypoints.note: Green Creek runs clear here at the entrance to the Green Creek Cirque — treat this as the last reliable water before the upper slabs and summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Connecting ridge gain point south of South Twin
waypoints.note: Loose, engaging 3rd/4th-class scrambling out of the cirque gains the ridge crest just south of South Twin; from here the route turns south along the connecting ridge to Skookum on grippy olivine.

waypoints.name: Skookum Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit (also known as 'Kloke Peak'); descend by reversing the ridge and climbers' path back to the Green Creek Cirque.

Approach shoes are adequate for the standard Class 3-4 line

backups.pro_needs: A light rack for protecting 5.4 moves on generally solid, positive rock; a 30m rope is carried for the rappel off Jaws' Tooth immediately before this section.
backups.best_season: July through September is the reliable window: rock is dry and at its grippiest, though north-aspect gullies and the approach can hold lingering snow into early July in heavy-snowpack years, and late-summer afternoons can bring thunderstorms or wildfire smoke. Road access overrides season as the limiting factor — FSR 38 has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, so check Mount Baker Ranger District alerts regardless of time of year.
backups.approach: From the Mount Baker Ranger District office in Sedro-Woolley, drive north on WA-9 to Acme, turn right (east) on Mosquito Lake Road for about 9 miles, cross the Middle Fork Nooksack River, and continue onto Forest Road 38 for roughly 11 miles to the Elbow Lake Trail's north trailhead (a separate trailhead from 'Pioneer Camp,' which is actually on the trail's south end via Baker Lake Highway/FSR 12). From there, follow Elbow Lake Trail #697 across the Middle Fork Nooksack and up to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, then pick up the unmaintained Green Creek climbers' path into the Green Creek Cirque beneath Skookum's north/east flank before gaining the ridge. This whole approach is compromised: FSR 38 was damaged in the December 2025 floods and has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since 27 July 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on 25 September 2026, and the unofficial log crossing with rope handrails over the Middle Fork Nooksack near the trailhead was also washed out — confirm current conditions with the Mount Baker Ranger District before driving in.
backups.descent_text: Descend by retracing the ascent ridge rather than dropping into the south-facing gullies and slopes, which are loose, choss-filled rock and a significant rockfall hazard to parties below. From the Green Creek Cirque, return via the climbers' path to the Elbow Lake Trail and out to the trailhead.
backups.bail: Descend the ridge into the Green Creek Cirque and walk out via the climbers' path and the Elbow Lake Trail.

itinerary.cal: Best done once the brushy approach and ridge are fully snow-free, typically mid-summer through early fall (roughly July-September).

days.note: This is a big single-day outing, not a backpack: parties hike the Elbow Lake Trail, ford the Middle Fork Nooksack and follow the blazed Green Creek climbers' path into the Green Creek Cirque, then scramble loose third and fourth class ground out of the cirque onto the ridge where the terrain turns to famously grippy olivine/dunite rock. The ridge itself is mostly 2nd-3rd class if you stay left/west of the crest, with short 3rd-4th class steps and real exposure near the top; route-finding (staying left, not straying right onto harder terrain) is the crux of the day as much as the climbing.
days.title: Car-to-car: Elbow Lake Trail and Green Creek Cirque + olivine ridge scramble

schedule.label: Leave the trailhead
schedule.detail: Start hiking in the dark to bank time; the Middle Fork Nooksack ford comes within the first quarter mile.

schedule.label: Leave the trail for the Green Creek path
schedule.detail: At a switchback near Hildebrand Creek the blazed climbers' path leaves the maintained trail and heads into the Green Creek Cirque.

schedule.label: Gain the ridge crest
schedule.detail: Forest opens onto exposed olivine/dunite rock; keep left (west side) of the crest for easier going.

schedule.label: Scramble to the summit
schedule.detail: 3rd-4th class sections with exposure; most parties top out by late morning to early afternoon.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the ridge and downclimb carefully - loose rock and exposure demand as much care going down as up.

schedule.label: Back at the car
schedule.detail: Retrace the Green Creek path and the Elbow Lake Trail, fording the Middle Fork again on the way out.

days.objective: Summit Skookum Peak via the Elbow Lake Trail, the Green Creek Cirque and the olivine (dunite) ridge

itinerary.totalNote: A long but standard single day: roughly 9-11 hours car-to-car, ~14 miles round trip and ~4,200 ft of gain, mixing a long trail and climbers'-path approach with 2nd-4th class ridge scrambling on grippy olivine rock.

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Cirque and the ridge from South Twin
approach_variants.notes: From the north trailhead of the Elbow Lake Trail, follow the maintained trail across the Middle Fork and up to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, where the unmaintained, sparsely blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' path leaves it — it is easy to walk past. The path climbs into the Green Creek Cirque; treat the creek at the cirque mouth as the last reliable water. Loose third and fourth class scrambling out of the cirque gains the ridge crest just south of South Twin, and the route then follows the connecting ridge south. The road and the river crossing at the trailhead have both been damaged by flooding, so confirm access before driving in.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, once the cirque slabs are dry
hazards: Unbridged Middle Fork crossing at the trailhead, unfordable at high flow
Loose third and fourth class ground gaining the ridge out of the cirque
Immense exposure on the knife-edge sections of the ridge itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: Skookum sits on the ridge running SOUTH from South Twin, and the tower immediately north of it is Jaws' Tooth — a slender detached spire that reads as a tooth rather than a summit and is the single best identifier on this stretch of crest. The base of Skookum's north ridge is the notch on the far, southern side of that tooth, and it is normally reached by rappelling off the tooth rather than by walking to it; that rappel is the proof, because the crest between South Twin and Skookum does not simply go on foot. The rock is the second confirmation: the whole ridge here is reddish-orange olivine, coarse and startlingly grippy, and the ridge above the notch climbs on small positive edges with big air on both sides. If you are still down in the green, stream-fed Green Creek Cirque looking up at slabs, you have not gained the crest. If the summit in front of you is the high point of the whole range with everything else below it, that is South Twin, not Skookum.

bivy.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
bivy.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.
bivy.water: Two springs of running water in the basin, plus Green Creek lower down. The most dependable water anywhere on the southeast side of the range and the reason this basin is used at all
bivy.permit: National forest, largely within the wilderness unit. Dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, no developed sites and no facilities. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the trailhead. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer. Access from this side does not cross the private timberland, but it does require fording the Middle Fork Nooksack, and the roads serving the trailhead have their own closures.
bivy.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out

backups.overview: Old Snowy Mountain sits on the Goat Rocks volcanic crest immediately next to the Pacific Crest Trail, at its highest point in Washington. It's one of the most accessible Goat Rocks summits precisely because the PCT does most of the elevation work: from Snowgrass Flats the trail climbs to an unsigned spur that leaves the PCT and switchbacks up scree and snow to a short, loose, mildly exposed Class 2-3 scramble at the top. The small McCall Glacier lies on the east face and a distinctive natural rock arch (~20 ft) stands near the summit. Old Snowy is frequently combined with a traverse to nearby Ives Peak.
backups.beta: From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead, hike ~4.7 miles through forest and meadows to the PCT, then follow the PCT north/west around the mountain's flank to its high point. Leave the PCT on an unsigned boot path that switchbacks up scree/talus to the northwest ridge and follows it south to the summit; the last ~50 feet is loose Class 2–3 rock with real but manageable exposure. An alternate line gains the col between Old Snowy and Ives Peak and follows the ridge crest/just-south-of-crest to the top.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before starting and stick to it — the exposed ridge and loose summit block are meaningfully more hazardous in afternoon thunderstorms, high wind, or when early-season snow is present, and the long trail approach means a late retreat can mean hiking out in the dark.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit at trailheads and ranger stations; Northwest Forest Pass or day fee at several trailheads.

backups.detailed_rack: No rack is needed — this is an unroped scramble. Trekking poles are widely used and typically stashed just below the final scramble; in early season (persistent snow on the PCT sidehill traverse and the climb up to the summit path) an ice axe and microspikes/traction devices are commonly carried for self-arrest and secure footing.
pro_tips: Many parties combine Old Snowy with Ives Peak as a one-day traverse (mostly Class 2, a few Class 3 moves); start from Old Snowy first to avoid climbing the looser scree slope below Ives
Fill water at Snowgrass Flats/Goat Lake before heading up onto the PCT — there is none higher on the route
Aim for an early summit to beat typical July-August afternoon thunderstorm buildup over the crest
watch_out: The summit spur trail is unsigned and easy to lose in poor visibility — don't wander off the PCT onto random scree
Blocks near the summit are loose underfoot; test holds before weighting them
The natural rock arch near the summit is a scenic landmark but the ground around it is loose and exposed — watch footing while photographing it
backups.pro_needs: No technical protection is used on the standard route — it is a trail hike to a Class 2–3 scramble finish. Trekking poles are commonly carried for the snowfields and loose talus.
backups.best_season: The PCT traverse below Old Snowy holds a persistent snowfield that is often the last big patch to melt out on the WA PCT's Washington crest, lingering into July in an average year and later in a heavy-snow year — carry an axe even in mid-summer if in doubt. Driest talus and the most stable weather windows are typically August into September, before the first fall storms (which have arrived as early as late September in some years). The FR-21/FR-2150 access road and Snowgrass Flats trail itself often hold snow into June, so early-season attempts should expect a full snow approach, not just a summit snowfield.
backups.approach: From the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (end of FR-2150, elev. ~4,600 ft), start on Trail 96 (Snowgrass Flat Trail). The first stretch climbs gently through forest for roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old Bypass Trail/Trail 96A (stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line). Around 2.4-2.6 miles in you'll hear and then reach the springs that form the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right - the last reliable, easy water source before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek itself; there's no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except during heavy snowmelt, when it can run fast enough to require care. Just beyond the ford (~3.9-4 miles, ~6,400 ft) the trail breaks out of forest into the open heather meadows and wildflower bogs of Snowgrass Flat, a scenic rest and water-filter stop before the climb — note that camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself under Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)); parties camp instead at designated sites above/below the flats. Continue past the Trail 97 junction (west to Cispus Basin/PCT) and the Trail 86 junction (Goat Lake), staying on the main track as it climbs in long benches with Mount Adams and the Goat Rocks opening up behind you. At about 4.7 miles the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 7,100 ft; turn right (north) onto the PCT. Follow the PCT north for about 1.8 miles, traversing rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill terrain on Old Snowy's west flank - snow patches can linger here into midsummer and may require an ice axe/traction for a secure traverse in early season. Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble: the last few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers. Total one-way distance is approximately 7.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain; round trip is roughly 15.5 miles, typically taking 8.5-9.5 hours car to car.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off, not a technical descent - there is no rappelling on the standard South Ridge/PCT route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 2-3 scramble off the summit block (the loose scree and blocky talus here is the descent crux - go slow, test holds, and stay alert for rock knocked loose by parties above or below you), then pick up the climbers' path back down to the PCT. From the PCT junction, follow the trail back south, again watching footing on any lingering snowfields on the exposed sidehill traverse below the ridge (these are firmest and safest to cross in the morning before they soften). Continue south on the PCT to the Trail 96 junction (~7,100 ft) and descend Trail 96 the way you came - back through Snowgrass Flat, across the Snowgrass Creek ford, past the spring/water source, and down through forest to the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead. No ropes, anchors, or rappel gear are needed for this route under normal summer conditions; a rope and basic glacier/snow travel gear are only warranted for early-season attempts with significant snow cover on the PCT traverse or summit scramble.
backups.bail: The route is entirely on/near the PCT until the final scramble; retreat at any point is simply reversing the boot path to the PCT and walking the PCT/Trail #96 back to the trailhead. There is no technical descent required to bail from the summit block.

pitch_detail.notes: ~4.7 mi, gentle forest and meadow hiking to the Pacific Crest Trail.
Follow PCT around Old Snowy's west/south flank, gaining benches with Adams/Goat Rocks views.
Unsigned spur path off PCT high point; loose rock, mild exposure in the final ~50 ft to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: Best mid-July through September; the PCT sidehill traverse below Snowgrass Flat often holds snow into July, and a free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead.

days.note: From the Snowgrass Flat trailhead (4,600 ft), climb through forest on Snowgrass Trail #96 into the flower meadows of Snowgrass Flat, then join the PCT and follow it north to the saddle below Old Snowy's west flank. Leave the PCT on a boot path and scramble loose Class 2 terrain to the summit, then reverse the entire route to the car.

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day car-to-car: about 14 miles round trip, 3,600 ft gain, typically 8-9.5 hours including a summit break.

access.fees: $5 per vehicle per day, or a $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass, required at the Snowgrass Flats (Trail #96) trailhead; payable by cash/check envelope, Recreation.gov Scan & Pay, or a valid Recreation Pass.
access.notes: Straddles Gifford Pinchot NF (west) and Okanogan-Wenatchee NF (east, White Pass side); the standard approach (Snowgrass Flat, Berry Patch trailheads) is on the Gifford Pinchot side.
access.rules: Group size (people plus stock) capped at 12. No camping at Snowgrass Flat itself or in Shoe Lake Basin, and no camping within 100 ft of any lakeshore. Campfires are banned in Shoe Lake Basin, at the Dana Yelverton Shelter, and within a quarter-mile of Goat Lake's shoreline. Leave No Trace / pack out all waste.
access.permit: Free, self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit at the Snowgrass Flats trailhead kiosk — no quota, reservation, or fee for the wilderness permit itself.
access.closures: Forest Road 21, the access road to Snowgrass Flats, was washed out near milepost 3 from US-12 in the December 2025 atmospheric-river floods (with a second washout reported further south); the Forest Service was still assessing repairs. Confirm current road status with the Cowlitz Valley Ranger District, (360) 497-1103, before driving in. FR-2150 is separately closed to wheeled vehicles roughly Dec 1–Apr 1 for winter recreation.
access.landManager: Gifford Pinchot National Forest — Cowlitz Valley Ranger District, 10024 US-12, Randle, WA 98377, (360) 497-1100
access.land_manager: Gifford Pinchot National Forest (Cowlitz Valley Ranger District) — Goat Rocks Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Required at both the Snowgrass Flat and Berry Patch trailheads — $5/day or $30/year Northwest Forest Pass.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead. Camping on Snowgrass Flat itself is prohibited; use the sites below it.

road.name: Forest Road 21 (FR-21) → FR-2150 → spur 2150-045 to Snowgrass Flats Trailhead #96
road.status: Normally passable in summer to a standard-clearance vehicle, but check current status — FR-21 sustained washout damage near milepost 3 in the December 2025 floods.
road.driveNote: From Packwood, go west on US-12 about 2.7 miles, turn south onto FR-21, follow it about 13 miles, bear onto FR-2150, then take spur 2150-045 to the trailhead (46.4644°N, -121.5178°W). The lot has a vault toilet and picnic tables but no potable water, and fills early on summer weekends (June–October); avoid parking along FR-2150 itself so it stays clear for emergency access.
road.seasonalGate: FR-2150 is gated to wheeled vehicles roughly December 1–April 1 for winter recreation, and snow typically blocks the road well before and after those dates in most years.

climate.typical: Cool, dry, wind-exposed high-Cascade-crest climate. Summer days are pleasant (60s-70s°F) but the ridge is fully exposed to wind, and afternoon thunderstorms are a real risk. Nights are near or below freezing even in August, and snow is possible in any month at this elevation.

bySeason.fall: Often calm and clear into early October in dry years, but the first snow can arrive by late September; expect short days and freezing nights.
bySeason.spring: Road and trail access to Snowgrass Flats is typically snowed in into June; above that, Old Snowy is essentially a full snow climb requiring axe and likely crampons.
bySeason.summer: Prime season, July through September; the PCT snowfield just below Old Snowy is usually the last big patch on this stretch to melt out and can linger into July.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible — FR-21/2150 gated and snowed in, and the peak becomes a full winter mountaineering objective on already loose, avalanche-prone terrain.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable throughout the Goat Rocks Wilderness — don't count on a signal even from the summit. Because the peak straddles the Lewis/Yakima county line, give precise location details (landmarks, GPS if available) when calling for help.
emergency.county: Lewis County, WA (the summit sits directly on the Lewis-Yakima county line)
emergency.rangerStation: Cowlitz Valley Ranger District, 10024 US-12, Randle, WA 98377 — (360) 497-1100 (front desk), (360) 497-1103 (road/trail conditions)
emergency.nearestHospital: Arbor Health – Morton Hospital (formerly Morton General Hospital), 521 Adams Ave, Morton, WA — 24-hour ER, roughly an hour's drive from the Snowgrass Flats trailhead via FR-21 and US-12
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Dial 911; Lewis County Sheriff's Office typically coordinates SAR on this side of the crest (Yakima County SAR may respond if an incident is on the east side of the county line).

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends late July through August, compounded by PCT thru-hiker traffic passing directly below the summit spur
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Moderate-high — Old Snowy is described by multiple trip-report sources as likely the most-visited summit in the Goat Rocks Wilderness, since an unsigned spur trail leaves the PCT right at its high point. Nearby Goat Lake/Snowgrass Flat camps see 40+ parties on peak summer weekends; the Old Snowy summit spur itself sees fewer but still frequent traffic, roughly a steady stream of parties (PCT thru-hikers plus dayhikers/scramblers) on summer weekends, thinning quickly on weekdays and after Labor Day.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Long summer day: approach via the PCT (from Snowgrass Flat, Berry Patch, or Chambers Lake trailheads) plus significant elevation gain before the final ridge scramble; fitness for a full, long trail day is required, though exact mileage/time was not independently re-verified in this pass.
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light summer daypack; add an ice axe (and optionally microspikes) for residual snow slopes, especially in July.

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long single day via the PCT corridor (multiple trailhead options); treat as a full-day objective — precise round-trip mileage/hours not confirmed
requiredSkills: Class 2 scree/loose-rock scrambling
comfort with exposure on a narrow, exposed ridge crest
snow slope travel and self-arrest with an ice axe (early-season lingering snow)
route-finding off the PCT onto the unofficial/spur summit path
afternoon-thunderstorm awareness and turnaround discipline on the exposed crest
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler comfortable with sustained Class 2 terrain, loose scree, and an exposed ridge crest near the top; not a beginner's first scramble given the crest exposure.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through August, tapering into a good but cooling window in September — to September.

July.reason: Snow is melting out per the best-season start; early July can still have lingering snow slopes on the ridge requiring an axe.

June.reason: Likely still holds substantial snow on approach and summit slopes; the snow-slope hazard is most acute here, and access roads may still be snow-blocked or just opening.

August.reason: Most snow-free, most stable trail conditions, and the peak crowd window — best balance of safe conditions against the highest traffic of the season.

September.reason: End of the best-season window; drier scree, fewer thunderstorms, but shorter days and increasing chance of early-season snow/weather resets late in the month.

weather.typical: Dry, clear summer alpine weather is typical July-September once snow has melted.
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a known hazard on this route, and are most consequential given the exposed crest near the summit — plan for an early start and a turnaround if storms build.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: The crest is exposed — a slip on the final loose, exposed section near the summit is the primary fall-consequence concern on this route, distinct from avalanche hazard.

avalanche.zone: NWAC West Slopes South (Goat Rocks lies within this forecast zone; NWAC's published forecast season is roughly Nov-May and does not cover this route's July-Sept climbing window)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel (this route stays on the ridge/scree/PCT approach and does not cross the small glaciers near Old Snowy)

gaps: Current repair status of the FR-21 washout (Dec 2025 floods) not confirmed — call the ranger district before a trip

No verified technical grade/pitch count for the Old Snowy–Ives Peak traverse extension beyond general trip-report descriptions

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (end of FR-2150, elev. ~4,600 ft), start on Trail 96 (Snowgrass Flat Trail).

backups.rope_note: Class 2-3 non-technical scramble via the PCT and northwest ridge in the Goat Rocks; well-graded trail to a short loose/exposed final scramble. No rope needed under normal summer conditions.
backups.corrections: Matches WTA/SummitPost/Oregon Hikers: 'nothing technical is required,' last ~100m is loose and slightly exposed but non-technical.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flat, the PCT north, and the unmarked climbers' path to the northwest ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead at about 4,600 ft at the end of the forest road, start on Trail 96. It climbs gently through forest roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old bypass trail — stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line.

Around 2.4 to 2.6 miles you reach the springs at the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right, the last easy water before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek; there is no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except in heavy snowmelt.

Just beyond the ford at about 3.9-4 miles and 6,400 ft the trail breaks into the open heather meadows of Snowgrass Flat. Camping is prohibited within the flat itself under wilderness regulations; parties camp at designated sites above or below it.

Continue past the two trail junctions to the PCT at roughly 7,100 ft and turn right, north. Follow the PCT about 1.8 miles across rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill on Old Snowy's west flank.

Round trip is roughly 15.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain, typically 8.5 to 9.5 hours car to car. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm before driving.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-Jul through Sep, most reliable in August
hazards: An unmarked, easily missed turn off the PCT — the route's one real navigation problem
A persistent snowfield on the PCT traverse below the summit, firm and icy in early morning
Loose rock and talus on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk to climbers below
High wind and lightning exposure on an open crest, with common afternoon thunderstorms
Route-finding difficulty in poor visibility once off the PCT
Unreliable cell coverage throughout the wilderness
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TURN OFF THE PCT IS UNMARKED, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING ON THIS ROUTE YOU CAN GET WRONG.

THE TEST THAT WORKS IN FOG IS ABOUT MOTION, NOT LANDMARKS: the PCT here is SIDEHILLING — traversing across the slope. The climbers' path is THE FIRST THING THAT TURNS UPHILL AND STOPS CONTOURING, branching right, east, toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge. Take the first thing that climbs.

THE NEGATIVE IS EQUALLY MECHANICAL: IF THE PCT STARTS DESCENDING ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE TURN. Go back; do not climb straight up from where you noticed.

DISTANCE CROSS-CHECK: about 1.8 miles north of the Trail 96 junction at 7,100 ft, and the path switchbacks steeply for about half a mile from where you leave the trail.

SECOND MARKER, AND IT SITS BEFORE THE TURN RATHER THAN AFTER IT: a persistent SNOWFIELD on the PCT below the summit lingers into July and is a well-documented trouble spot on the exposed sidehill traverse. Meeting it means the turn is still ahead of you. It is firmest and safest crossed in the morning.

A SOFT CONFIRMATION AT THE SADDLE, WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS VISIBLE FROM A DISTANCE: many parties stash trekking poles there for the scramble. A cache of poles on a rocky saddle is a good sign you are at the right one.

BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE: the last few hundred feet to the summit is Class 2-3 hands-and-feet on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rock knocked down by parties above is the hazard, so do not stack directly below other climbers.

AND A NEGATIVE THAT IS ABOUT VISIBILITY RATHER THAN GROUND: once you leave the PCT there is no maintained tread. Poor visibility is the recorded route-finding difficulty on this peak, and the honest response is to turn round at the PCT rather than to search for the spur.

climbing_route.label: Climbers' path to the northwest-ridge saddle
climbing_route.notes: Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble.

climbing_route.label: Final few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit
climbing_route.notes: The last few hundred feet are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers.

bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Goat Lake basin
bivy.notes: The other basin camp on this side, reached by the loop that swings north from the Snowgrass trail, and a reasonable alternative when the Snowgrass sites are taken. It sits under Old Snowy's western flank and is slightly further from the crest than Snowgrass, which costs you distance on a summit morning but buys a quieter night. The basin is a cirque and holds snow late, so early-season parties frequently find the lake iced and the campsites buried — the trade for a genuinely alpine setting. Vegetation here is fragile and slow-growing, which is why the existing sites are the only acceptable ones.
bivy.water: The lake, plus outlet streams; the lake can stay partly frozen into midsummer, in which case take water from the outlet
bivy.permit: Same free self-issued wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass as the rest of this trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED within a quarter mile of the lake shore, so bring a stove and do not plan on a fire. The 100-foot setback from lakes applies here and is actively enforced by the condition of the ground.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of established sites scattered back from the shore; the closest ground to the water is off limits, which cuts the usable count sharply

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

bivy.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
bivy.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.
bivy.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock

backups.name: Standard Route (Northeast summit via Crystal Pass)
backups.fa: Unknown; first ascent of peak 1939 by David Harrah party
backups.season: Jun-Sep (snow-dependent; best attempted early-to-mid season while the couloir/defile still holds snow bridging the moats)
hazards: Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
Exposed roped climbing including a steep, committing chimney/roof section ('cave of despair' in trip reports)
Easy to be drawn onto the wrong (southwest) summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
Deep moats bordering the snow finger in the South Gully/defile, requiring repeated stemming between snow and rock to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the gully as the day warms — a documented incident involved a refrigerator-size block breaking loose and striking a climber
backups.overview: Inner Constance (7,672 ft by LiDAR) is the fifth-highest summit in the Olympic Mountains, a rugged pyramid just west of Mount Constance (its line parent, 0.9 mi east) across the glacially carved Avalanche Canyon, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. The mountain is built of Eocene tilted pillow basalt, rotten and loose throughout. David Harrah's party is credited with the first ascent in 1939. The commonly described standard line climbs out of Avalanche Canyon via a South Gully/snow-filled defile to the East Ridge ('Route 2A') rather than via nearby Crystal Pass, which is a separate saddle/viewpoint climbers sometimes visit instead when they bail on the summit. Climbers occasionally report uncertainty about whether they've reached the true high point versus a nearby sub-summit in the Olympics' notorious cloud cover.
backups.beta: From Lake Constance, ascend Avalanche Canyon on climber paths and snow patches to a broad couloir below The Thumb landmark. Ascend the broad couloir on firm snow, veering right into a steeper secondary couloir. Follow a narrow, snow-filled defile on the right side, featuring a hard snow finger with moats. At higher elevations, climb a steep snow gully with discontinuous snow finger, stemming out to rock and scrambling up the moat. Gain the east ridge crest via a final pitch of Class 3 rock, then follow Class 2-3 scrambling on solid pillow basalt to the summit. Route 2A is described as excellent when snow is firm; when snow melts in late summer, the underlying scree becomes unpleasantly loose.
backups.turnaround: Turn around if: (1) snow conditions in the defile/gully become unsafe with excessive rockfall or avalanche debris; (2) you are not at the east ridge crest by mid-afternoon, as darkness will prevent safe scrambling; (3) weather deteriorates with heavy precipitation or lightning risk; (4) any team member shows signs of altitude sickness, exhaustion, or inability to move safely.
backups.face: South Gully and East Ridge, above Avalanche Canyon
backups.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
backups.comms: Cell service is unreliable in the canyon and at higher elevations of Olympic National Park. Satellite messengers (InReach, Garmin) are recommended for emergency communication. The Dosewallips River drainage receives poor to no cellular coverage.
backups.descent: Reverse the South Gully–East Ridge line: scramble back down the East Ridge, down-climb/rappel the Class 3-4 rock step at the notch, then descend the snow finger through the gully, staying alert for moats on both sides and for wet-day rockfall/collapsing snow blocks (a documented near-miss involved a refrigerator-size block of sliding snow). Published descriptions note this line (Route 2A) as a workable descent option back to Avalanche Canyon and Lake Constance.

waypoints.name: Dosewallips Road washout parking (FR-2610)
waypoints.note: Vehicle-accessible road end at the 2002 washout (~8.5 mi from Hwy 101); self-issue wilderness permit kiosk here before biking/hiking the closed roadbed.
waypoints.directions: Drive Dosewallips Road inland from US-101, roughly 8.5 miles, to the vehicle-accessible road end at the 2002 washout. Fill in a self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk before starting up the closed roadbed.

waypoints.name: Lake Constance Trailhead
waypoints.note: Unmaintained climbers' path splits off the old Dosewallips roadbed and climbs steeply up the narrow Constance Creek canyon; unsigned and easy to walk past.
waypoints.directions: The road beyond has been closed to motor vehicles since the 2002 flood but stays open to foot and bicycle, and most parties ride it; a short riverside bypass gets around the washed-out section before the old roadbed resumes. About 5 miles up, an unmaintained climbers' path splits off the roadbed and starts up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. It is unsigned and easy to walk straight past, so watch for it.

waypoints.name: Creekside Camp Bench
waypoints.note: Trail briefly levels crossing the valley floor beside Constance Creek; flat spot with an established fire ring and reliable running water, a common rest/camp break before the final steep push.
waypoints.directions: The climbers' path climbs steeply and directly up the canyon, unmaintained and choked with blowdown, and this lower section is the hardest walking of the trip. At around 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels out on the valley floor beside Constance Creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and reliable running water.

waypoints.name: Lake Constance
waypoints.note: Emerald backcountry lake cupped in a rock bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon; camping permits are quota-limited, so use existing sites to protect the fragile basin.
waypoints.directions: From the bench the path resumes its steep push, gaining the last 1,700 ft to the lake at 4,800 ft, cupped in a rock bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon. Camping is quota-limited, so use the existing sites.

waypoints.name: Avalanche Canyon / The Thumb
waypoints.note: Barren, rocky Avalanche Canyon opens north from the lake, a stark contrast to the rainforest below; the Thumb rock formation marks where the South Chute (Mount Constance) and South Gully (Inner Constance) lines diverge on faint, intermittent climbers' track.
waypoints.directions: Head north out of the lake basin into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in contrast to the rainforest below, on faint and intermittent climbers' track and snow patches. Continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb, the rock formation that marks where the South Chute on Mount Constance and the South Gully on Inner Constance diverge.

waypoints.name: South Defile Snow Choke
waypoints.note: Snow-filled defile narrows to a roughly 2-ft gap with 5-10 ft deep moats opening on each side by mid-late season; parties have reported refrigerator-size snow blocks calving here, so move through quickly and probe snow bridges before committing.
waypoints.directions: From the mouth of the canyon follow the faint, intermittent climbers' track and snow patches north up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb, then take the Inner Constance branch and veer right into a steeper secondary couloir that narrows into the defile. Snow blocks calve out of this constriction as the day warms, so move through it quickly and probe the bridges over the moats before committing weight to them.

waypoints.name: East Ridge Notch
waypoints.note: A steep, discontinuous snow finger tops out at this notch on Inner Constance's East Ridge; a short Class 3 rock step gains the ridge crest before the summit scramble.
waypoints.directions: Above the defile the gully continues on discontinuous snow, with repeated stemming between the snow finger and the rock walls to get around the moats and a few short up- and downclimbs on rock where the snow runs out. A steep snow finger tops out at the notch; exit the gully onto the crest by way of a short Class 3-4 rock step.

waypoints.name: Inner Constance
waypoints.note: True summit (7,672 ft), the Olympics' 4th/5th-highest peak; final approach is fun Class 2-3 scrambling on pillow basalt along the East Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the East Ridge crest from the notch on Class 2-3 scrambling over pillow basalt to the top. Rock across this massif is notoriously rotten, so keep the party tight and out of each other's fall line. Do not let the line pull you toward the southwest summit — it has no easy connection across to the true northeast high point.

sectionBreakdown.note: From the Dosewallips Road washout, bike or walk the closed road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' path, then climb it steeply to camp at Lake Constance.
An alpine start on firm snow up a broad couloir into a narrow, moat-lined snow defile, then a steep discontinuous snow finger gaining the East Ridge. From the ridge it's a Class 2-…
Break camp and reverse the approach, dropping back down toward the Dosewallips River trail and out to the trailhead (or bike cache, given the road washout closure). Mostly downhill…

backups.detailed_rack: A rope and a light-to-moderate alpine rack (nuts, small-to-mid cams, slings) for the exposed low-5th-class pitches; ice axe and possibly crampons for the snowfield/small glacier depending on conditions.
pro_tips: Navigate carefully to the northeast summit — the southwest point is a dead end.
Move early to avoid afternoon rockfall on the snowfield.
Treat every hold as suspect and helmet up for the whole upper route.
backups.watch_out:
Rotten rock and rockfall hazard throughout upper peak—pillow basalt severely weathered; continuous hazard from loosening rocks; stay alert and compact; helmet mandatory
Exposed chimney/roof pitch on upper pitches—significant protection challenge on friable rock; runout potential if placements fail; requires confident climbing and careful anchor placement
Navigation to correct NE summit complicated by multiple peaks—wrong summit selection can add hours and difficulty; study photos and use GPS; false summits create fatigue and disorientation
Steep snow and small glacier high on route—transition from rock to snow/ice can be hazardous; assess conditions and have appropriate tools (ice axe, crampons); late season bare ice or crevasse exposure
Crystal Pass crossing—bergschrund potential; late season route-finding confusion; always probe and belay uncertain snow/ice crossings
Altitude exposure with sustained climbing—7700+ feet with continuous elevation gain; altitude sickness possible; acclimatization and hydration essential
Weather exposure on open ridge traverse—afternoon storms common in Olympics; exposed position dangerous with lightning; start pre-dawn
Descent terrain equally demanding—route-finding on descent must-do; darkness increases risk; maintain focus on descent line throughout climb
backups.pro_needs: Protection for several exposed Class 4 / low-5th-class pitches on poor rock, including the steep chimney/roof move below the summit.
backups.best_season: Late June through July is favored while the South Gully/defile still holds consolidated snow, which makes the ascent line far more secure; by August the snow largely melts out and the same gully becomes unpleasantly loose rock and scree (per first-hand trip reports), still climbable but harder and looser. The approach trail to Lake Constance is generally passable from late June into September.
backups.approach: From the Dosewallips River Road washout (~700 ft) — the road has been closed to motor vehicles since a 2002 flood but stays open to foot and bicycle travel — most parties bike the closed roadbed, getting around the washed-out section on a riverside bypass. Several miles up, an unsigned, unmaintained climbers' path leaves the roadbed and climbs very steeply up the narrow Constance Creek canyon: roughly 3,300 ft in about 2 miles, choked with blowdown in its lower part and with some hands-on scrambling higher up, past a small creekside bench near 3,100 ft, to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft, the usual camp (a wilderness permit is needed and the lake is a quota area). From the lake, head north into barren Avalanche Canyon on a faint, intermittent climbers' track and snow patches to the broad couloir below the Thumb, where the South Chute of Mount Constance and the South Gully of Inner Constance part ways. A much longer alternative follows the closed road to its old end, climbs the Constance Pass Trail and crosses Crystal Pass into the head of Avalanche Canyon; it avoids the Lake Constance path's steep lower section. Expect a 2–3 day trip either way.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: scramble back down the East Ridge to the notch, downclimb or rappel the short rock step into the gully, then descend the discontinuous snow finger and the South Defile, watching for moats on both sides and for snow blocks that loosen as the day warms. Where the snow is firm and runs out safely, the lower couloir can be plunge-stepped or glissaded. Loose rock is a hazard the whole way off the summit, so keep the party close together and out of each other's fall line. From the broad couloir below the Thumb, walk back down Avalanche Canyon to Lake Constance, then descend the steep climbers' path and the closed Dosewallips Road to the washout.
backups.bail: Retreat is by rappelling and reversing the route; there is no quick escape. Bail from below the technical climbing if weather or rockfall conditions are poor.

pitch_detail.notes: From Lake Constance, ascend Avalanche Canyon (barren, rocky terrain) toward the base of the route below Crystal Pass and 'The Thumb'.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to the South Gully
approach_variants.notes:
The shorter of the two ways in, at roughly 8 miles one-way. Bike or walk about 5 miles of closed Dosewallips Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,425 ft, then the steep unmaintained boot path up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. At roughly 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels on the valley floor beside the creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and running water — a common rest stop. From there the last 1,700 ft to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camping at the lake is quota-limited.

From the lake head north into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in stark contrast to the rainforest below, on faint intermittent climbers' track and snow patches, and continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and snow-dependent in a way most Olympic scrambles are not — this line wants snow still bridging the moats in the defile, so early to mid season is better than late
hazards: Deep moats on both sides of the snow finger in the South Gully defile, needing repeated stemming to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the constriction as the day warms — a documented injury
Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with rockfall on warm days
Easy to be drawn onto the southwest summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
The Lake Constance trail is one of the steepest and least maintained in the range
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THIS CLIMB IS A FORK, AND THE FORK IS MARKED BY A ROCK FORMATION CALLED THE THUMB. Head up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb. That is where the South Chute (which belongs to MOUNT Constance) and the South Gully (which belongs to INNER Constance, this route) diverge. Two summits sit above one canyon and the Thumb is the thing that tells the two lines apart.

THE FOG TEST THAT DOES NOT NEED THE THUMB, AND IT IS THE BETTER ONE, IS THE SHAPE OF THE GULLY YOU END UP IN. From the broad couloir, veer RIGHT into a steeper secondary couloir, which narrows into a snow-filled DEFILE. That defile constricts to roughly a two-foot gap with moats five to ten feet deep opening on either side of the snow by mid-to-late season. Nothing else in this canyon does that. If your gully stays broad and open all the way up, you are in the Mount Constance South Chute and climbing the wrong peak.

SECOND TEST, higher: above the defile the snow finger goes discontinuous and you stem repeatedly between snow and rock to get round the moats, with short up- and downclimbs on rock where the snow runs out. A steep finger tops out at a notch on the East Ridge near 7,200 ft, gained by a short Class 3-4 rock step. If you are still on continuous snow with no stemming, you have not reached the defile yet.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, AND IT IS THE RECORDED WAY THIS ROUTE GOES WRONG: from the East Ridge the line pulls naturally toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which has no easy connection across to the true NORTHEAST high point. Follow the East Ridge crest on Class 2-3 pillow basalt to the northeast top; if the ridge you are on is running away southwest, you are heading for the wrong summit.

SAFETY NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE ROUTE-FINDING: snow blocks calve out of the defile constriction as the day warms — a refrigerator-sized block struck a climber there. Move through it quickly and probe the bridges over the moats before weighting them.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then Crystal Basin and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16 miles one-way and worth it to some parties precisely because it avoids the Lake Constance trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section. From the Dosewallips washout at roughly 600 ft, bike or walk the closed roadbed — working round the washout on a riverside bypass — past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail and climb south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. The upper stretch is steep open meadow and scree, with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and climb to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif that divides the Dosewallips side from Avalanche Canyon. Expect a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow below Crystal Pass is safe
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass; unmarked talus, scree and snow between there and Constance Pass
Notoriously rotten pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
A steep, committing chimney and roof section high on the peak that trip reports call the cave of despair
Being drawn onto the southwest summit
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CRYSTAL PASS THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS DIRECTLY BELOW YOU RATHER THAN ABOVE YOU, WHICH IS THE ONE REAL ADVANTAGE OF THIS SIDE. Descend south into upper Avalanche Canyon on the intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, keeping to the RIGHT (north) side of the canyon, past the Thumb, and then contour and climb toward Inner Constance's northeast side.

THE TEST IS STILL THE THUMB AND THE DEFILE, and it still works from above: the fork you want is the one where the South Gully leaves the broad couloir and veers into a steeper secondary couloir that NARROWS to a two-foot gap with deep moats. Coming from Crystal Pass you can also take the northeast side directly — a short step just above the pass leads into a rising traverse along the RIGHT side of the north ridge crest, broken blocky Class 2-3 with occasional Class 4 and low fifth where the crest steepens.

THE FOG TEST FOR THAT NORTHEAST LINE IS WHICH SIDE OF THE CREST YOU ARE ON. Stay on the crest's RIGHT-hand side as you climb. If you have crossed over and are traversing on the other flank, you are off the line, and the rock over there is worse.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the same trap as the other variant — the mountain pulls toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which does not connect easily to the true northeast high point. Keep working toward the NORTHEAST top.

HONEST LIMIT: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and early-season snow with real route-finding demands. A rope and axe may be prudent on the snow remnant below the pass early in the year.

backups.approach: The Wilson Glacier sits on the east side of Mount Adams, descending from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft — a less-visited, less-documented flank than the standard south or north-side routes. Parties reach it via the Cold Springs/South Climb trailhead (5,600 ft, FS Rd 8040 off FS Rd 80): follow the South Climb Trail #183 about 1 mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail, then instead of continuing north toward Lunch Counter, follow Round the Mountain Trail east below Crescent Glacier onto Yakama Nation land, where a separate tribal permit is required and the trail ends at Hellroaring Canyon; the way on, north around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Wilson/Klickitat glacier basins, is a long off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands. Given the route's distance (~27 km) and gain (6,700 ft) roughly match the other long approach routes on this mountain, expect a full day just to reach a camp near the toe of the Wilson Glacier before a summit attempt.
backups.descent_text: The descent reverses back down the South Climb to Cold Springs: after topping out via the headwall, parties traverse over toward the summit plateau and descend the standard South Climb route (non-technical snow/scree walk-off, good glissading in early season) back to Lunch Counter and out to the Cold Springs trailhead — a different, easier line than the ascent. This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent. Because the Wilson Glacier Headwall itself is steep snow/ice below cliff bands, a party that needs to bail mid-face rather than finish over the top could reasonably rope down using pickets or V-threads in snow/ice, but this would be an improvised retreat, not a documented standard rappel.

approach_variants.name: Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain Trail east around the mountain
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cold Springs and South Climb trailhead at about 5,600 ft at the end of the forest road north of Trout Lake, follow South Climb Trail #183 about a mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail.

Instead of continuing north toward the Lunch Counter, follow the Round the Mountain Trail east and then north, contouring below the Crescent Glacier and around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Wilson and Klickitat glacier basins. This is a long, mostly off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands.

The Wilson descends from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft, and it is split by a rock rib. Expect a full day to reach a camp near its toe before any summit attempt.

This is one of the least-visited and least-documented flanks of the mountain. The descent is not a reversal: parties top out and come down the standard South Climb to Cold Springs.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION HAPPENS ABOUT A MILE FROM THE CAR AND IT IS A TURNING, NOT AN ARRIVAL. At the junction of the South Climb Trail with the Round the Mountain Trail, the standard South Spur route goes NORTH toward the Lunch Counter; this route goes EAST. If you are climbing toward the Lunch Counter, you are on the standard South Climb and this route is already behind you.

THAT IS THE ONE ERROR WORTH GUARDING, BECAUSE IT IS RECOVERABLE ONLY BY WALKING BACK DOWN. Everything after it is a long contour.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS A GLACIER SPLIT BY A ROCK RIB. The Wilson runs from about 10,600 ft down to about 7,400 ft and a rock rib divides it. A headwall above a glacier that is bisected by a rib is the confirmation. An unbroken glacier with no rib in it is not the Wilson.

THE SECOND POSITIVE IS ASPECT AND IT IS THE COARSEST BUT MOST RELIABLE: you must be on the EAST side of the mountain. Going around the eastern flank is the whole approach. If the sun is rising behind the mountain rather than in front of you, you have not come far enough round.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS FOR SAFETY RATHER THAN NAVIGATION: the contour runs directly beneath cliff bands that shed rock. It is a place to keep moving. Persistent rockfall on these east-side headwalls is among the reasons most of them remain unrepeated, so a rope-length of comfortable ground is not evidence the ground above you is quiet.

WHAT BEING ON A NEIGHBOURING BASIN LOOKS LIKE: keep going round and you reach the Klickitat basin. The Wilson is the first of the two you meet coming from the south.

bivy.name: Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead
bivy.notes: Most South Climb parties sleep here the night before, either to acclimatise a little or to get an alpine start without carrying a camp to the Lunch Counter. Facilities are primitive — a vault toilet, no piped water, no developed fee sites. Access is FR 80 to FR 8040 and then FR 8040-500, roughly eight miles of washboarded and rutted gravel with the last three miles steep, narrow and switchbacked; ordinary cars get up it at low speed but a low-slung vehicle can bottom out, and RVs and trailers should not attempt it. The road generally opens around mid-May and is usually clear of snow by the start of July, so early-season parties should expect to park lower and walk.
bivy.water: Unreliable. Treat this as a dry camp and arrive with water. Small springs and Morrison Creek near the road can be running early in the season and gone by late summer.
bivy.permit: A recreation pass is required to park — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or a day pass; a valid Mt. Adams Climbing Pass parking stub also works between May 1 and Sept 30. Camping here is below the 7,000 ft climbing-pass threshold, so a free self-issued wilderness permit covers you unless you go above that line. Waste bags are usually stocked at the trailhead.

backups.overview: A twin-summited peak in the Skagit Range of the North Cascades, directly across the Nooksack River valley from Mount Shuksan and just south of Mount Larrabee, within the Mount Baker Wilderness. The standard route follows USFS Trail #673 through old-growth forest and heather meadows to a ridge crest, then continues off-trail up a steep, loose scramblers' path to the false (west, ~6,600 ft) and true (east, 6,891 ft) summits. It's popular both as a strenuous day hike/scramble and as a backpacking or spring ski-touring objective, and is one of the first Baker Highway trails to melt out each year because of its south exposure.
backups.beta: This route continues past the West Peak false summit to the higher East Peak (6,891 ft), the mountain's true summit. The maintained trail ends on the shoulder near 5,400-5,600 ft; everything above is unmaintained boot path and open scrambling. The route involves a steep permanent snowfield traverse requiring an ice axe at all times, then a short, relatively straightforward scramble to the top. The route offers commanding views of Mount Baker, Mount Shuksan, Mount Sefrit, and the surrounding North Cascades peaks.
backups.turnaround: An early alpine start is essential; any party not reaching the summit ridge by early afternoon should turn around and descend to avoid travel in darkness on steep, exposed terrain. Never traverse the permanent snowfield after 3:00 PM given the additional darkness risk.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Mount Baker Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: Cellular service is unreliable to non-existent in the Mount Baker Wilderness. Satellite messengers (Garmin inReach or similar) are strongly recommended for wilderness areas. The trailhead is approximately 46 miles from Bellingham.
backups.descent: Reverse the ascent ridge and trail. The loose, exposed scrambling near the true summit and the steep, unmaintained goat path down to the maintained trail's end are the trickiest sections to downclimb carefully, especially on wet rock or lingering snow; many parties turn around at the easier 6,600 ft false (west) summit rather than continue the exposed ridge to the true 6,891 ft summit.

waypoints.name: Goat Mountain Trailhead
waypoints.note: On FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Rd) 2.1 mi off SR 542; Northwest Forest Pass required, vault toilet and parking on both sides of the road.
waypoints.directions: Reach the trailhead via Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32), off SR 542 near Glacier, about two miles up from the Glacier Public Service Center. Day-use parking is on both sides of the road, with a vault toilet on site, and a Northwest Forest Pass is required.

waypoints.name: Mt. Baker Wilderness Boundary / Old Goat Trail split
waypoints.note: Trail enters the Mt. Baker Wilderness here; an unsigned climbers' path ("Old Goat Trail") splits east toward a former lookout site — stay on the main trail.
waypoints.directions: Goat Mountain Trail #673 climbs steeply and almost without let-up from the trailhead, switchbacking through old-growth fir and hemlock and crossing a small cascading creek several times in the first mile. Around 3,200 ft the grade eases and the tread traverses onto a narrow side-hill ridge. The wilderness boundary sign is on that ridge; just past it an unsigned spur splits east toward an old lookout site, so stay on the main tread.

waypoints.name: 5,200-ft Knob
waypoints.note: Open alpine meadows and huckleberries (in season) around this viewpoint knob, with clear sightlines to Baker, Shuksan, and Sefrit.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing on maintained trail as forest gives way to heather and huckleberry meadows and the views south to Baker, Shuksan and Sefrit open up. The trail gains the ridge crest at the viewpoint knob.

waypoints.name: End of maintained Trail 673
waypoints.note: Trail 673 officially terminates on the ridge crest at 5,600 ft; beyond here toward the East Peak is an unmaintained, unmarked boot path.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest a little farther to where the maintained tread officially ends. There is no reliable water anywhere above the creek crossings low on the trail, so carry what you need from the forest crossings unless you are dropping into the basin below the East Peak, where a creek runs.

waypoints.name: Basin below the East Peak
waypoints.note: Drop roughly 300 ft over steep, slick vegetation into this basin; a creek provides the best water and camping on the route before the final push.
waypoints.directions: The end of the trail overlooks a basin to the east, directly under the East Peak. Getting into it means dropping roughly 300 ft down steep, densely vegetated ground that is treacherously slick when wet — this drop, and regaining it on the way out, is the hardest ground of the day to move on. A creek runs through the basin bottom.

waypoints.name: Summit gully
waypoints.note: Class 2 gully narrows with exposure dropping away on both sides near the top; stay centered in the gully rather than skirting the edges.
waypoints.directions: Cross the creek and head up toward the East Peak, picking up an easy class 2 gully. Snow lingers in it into summer, so carry an axe and be ready to self-arrest. Near the top the gully narrows and the ground falls away on both sides — stay centred in it rather than drifting out onto the edges.

waypoints.name: Goat Mountain, East Peak (true summit)
waypoints.note: Rocky, narrow summit spine dropping off steeply on all sides; USGS Mount Sefrit quad benchmark, higher than the West Peak across the basin.
waypoints.directions: Finish up the gully onto the summit spine. It is narrow and rocky, drops off steeply on every side, and the rock near the top is loose.

backups.approach: From the Goat Mountain Trailhead (day-use parking just off FS-32/Hannegan Pass Rd, ~2.1-2.3 mi up from the Glacier Public Service Center), follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It's a well-built but relentlessly steep trail that gains the ridge via dozens of switchbacks, crossing a small cascading creek/waterfall repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock (look for ~100-year-old fire-scarred cedar snags). Around 1 mi (~3,200 ft) the grade eases and the trail traverses onto a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly 2 mi the trail crosses into Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur ('Old Goat Trail') splits east toward an old lookout site - stay on the main tread. Big views of Baker, Shuksan, and Sefrit open through meadows by 2.7 mi, and the maintained trail tops out on the ridge crest at a 5,200-ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft (~4.1 mi, ~3,100 ft gain). Beyond this point the route leaves maintained tread and becomes an open ridge boot path: continue about 0.8 mi and 1,000 ft more to the ~6,600-ft West Peak false summit. Snow lingers here well into summer (reports note solid snow from ~4,300-4,500 ft), so carry an ice axe from around that elevation upward, and expect crampons or snowshoes to be useful in early/late season. Do not push straight over the false summit's top - it corniced and exposed; bypass it on the south or west slope. Past the false summit the ridge drops roughly 300 ft into a notch/col, then climbs the final stretch of mixed snow, rock, and short exposed steps to the true (East) summit at 6,892 ft. A narrow, moderately exposed knife-edge-ish section near the top is the crux of the scramble - keep the axe in hand and self-arrest-ready on the steep snow. There is no reliable water source beyond the creek crossings in the forest (roughly the first 2.5 miles of trail); carry what you need for the ridge and summit push.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route - reverse the ascent line exactly. Downclimb the mixed snow/rock crux back to the col, climb back over (or bypass around, staying off the cornices) the West Peak false summit, and regain the boot path down to the official trail terminus near 5,600 ft. From there, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673's switchbacks back down through the meadows, past the wilderness-boundary/Old Goat Trail junction, and through the old-growth section to the trailhead. Carry an ice axe and know self-arrest for both directions of travel on the snow sections: afternoon sun can soften the snowfields significantly (increasing slip and post-holing risk on the way down), while morning refreeze can leave the same slopes firm enough to want careful cramponing. Give cornices along the ridge crest a wide margin on the way down as well - they are easy to underestimate from above and have caused parties to detour off-route.
backups.bail: Reversible at any point on the nontechnical terrain.

pitch_detail.notes: Established trail through old-growth forest with switchbacks. ~5 miles roundtrip to maintained trail terminus (5,400 feet). Forest section may be muddy in late spring.
Off-trail scrambling through heather, talus, and alpine meadow. Route-finding required. Climbing directly toward snowfield below West Peak. Loose talus requires careful footing.
Steep permanent snowfield traverse (~400-500 vertical feet) requiring ice axe and crampons/microspikes. This is the crux pitch; fall here is potentially fatal. Angle ~40-45 degrees.
Summit scramble on exposed Class 2-3 terrain with some exposure. Final 100-150 vertical feet to the East Peak summit. No technical rock climbing but scrambling is exposed with 500+ foot drops nearby.

itinerary.cal: A permanent snowfield often lingers near the summit gully into summer, so many parties carry an ice axe even late in the season.

approach_variants.notes:
From the Goat Mountain Trailhead, day-use parking just off FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Road) about 2.1-2.5 miles up from the Glacier Public Service Center, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It is well built and relentlessly steep, gaining the ridge by dozens of switchbacks and crossing a small cascading creek repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock.

Around a mile in, near 3,200 ft, the grade eases and the trail traverses a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly two miles it crosses into the Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur — the Old Goat Trail — splits east toward an old lookout site. Stay on the main tread.

Meadows and big views open by 2.7 miles; the maintained trail tops out on the crest at a 5,200 ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft.

Beyond that it is an open ridge boot path, about 0.8 mile and 1,000 ft more to the West Peak false summit near 6,600 ft, and then on to the true East summit.

There is no reliable water beyond the creek crossings in the forest, roughly the first 2.5 miles of trail.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS WHERE THE MAINTAINED TRAIL STOPS, NEAR 5,600 FT, AND THAT END IS ABRUPT. Below it, built tread and switchbacks. Above it, an open ridge boot path with nothing constructed. If you are still on graded trail you have not started the route.

THE FALSE SUMMIT IS CORNICED — DO NOT GO OVER ITS TOP. This is the one hard rule on the ridge and it is a safety instruction rather than a route preference: the West Peak at about 6,600 ft is corniced and exposed, and the correct line bypasses it on the SOUTH or WEST slope. Cornices are invisible from above and this is precisely the terrain where cloud sits.

THE 300 FT DROP IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU HAVE PASSED THE FALSE SUMMIT, AND IT IS THE STRONGEST TEST ON THE ROUTE. Past the West Peak the ridge DROPS ROUGHLY 300 FT into a notch before climbing again. So: if you have not descended 300 ft, the high ground in front of you is not the true summit — it is the false one you were supposed to walk around. An altimeter settles this in zero visibility and eyesight does not.

AFTER THE NOTCH it is a final stretch of mixed snow, rock and short exposed steps to the true East summit at 6,892 ft. The crux is a narrow, moderately exposed knife-edge-ish section near the top — keep the axe in hand and self-arrest-ready on the steep snow.

CARRY THE AXE FROM 4,300-4,500 FT, not from where the snow looks serious. That is where reports put the solid snow, and it is well below the point where a party without an axe realises it wanted one.
